content: The text provided is a highly detailed and technical summary of various systematic reviews and meta-analyses related to interventions in preterm or low birth weight infants. 1. Zinc Supplementation vs. No Zinc Supplementation A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by Sinha B, Dudeja N, Chowdhury R, et al., evaluated the effects of enteral zinc supplementation in preterm or low birth weight infants. The study assessed outcomes such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The overall certainty of evidence was determined, with findings indicating a reduction of 76 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 91 fewer to 38 fewer cases). The source is Pediatrics 2022;150(Suppl 1):2022-057092I. 2. Vitamin D Supplementation vs. No Vitamin D Supplementation Kumar M, Shaikh S, Sinha B, et al., conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on enteral vitamin D supplementation in preterm or low birth weight infants. The study evaluated the same parameters as above, with findings showing an increase of 23 more cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 216 fewer to 232 more cases). The source is Pediatrics 2022;150(Suppl 1):2022-057092K. 3. Vitamin A Supplementation vs. No Vitamin A Supplementation Manapurath RM, Kumar M, Pathak BG, et al., reviewed the effects of low-dose enteral vitamin A supplementation in preterm or low birth weight infants to prevent morbidity and mortality. The findings indicated a reduction of 54 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 110 fewer to 52 more cases). The source is Pediatrics 2022;150(Suppl 1):2022-057092L. 4. Calcium and Phosphorus Supplementation vs. No Supplementation Kumar M, Chowdhury R, Sinha B, et al., analyzed the impact of enteral calcium or phosphorus supplementation in preterm or low birth weight infants. The findings showed an increase of 27 more cases per 1000 infants. The source is Pediatrics 2022;150(Suppl 1):2022-057092M. 5. Multiple Micronutrient (MMN) Supplementation vs. No MMN Supplementation Kumar M, Chowdhury R, Sinha B, et al., conducted a systematic review on enteral multiple micronutrient supplementation in preterm and low birth weight infants. The findings indicated an increase of 29 more cases per 1000 infants. The source is Pediatrics 2022;150(Suppl 1):2022-057092N. 6. Probiotics vs. No Probiotics Sharif S, Meader N, Oddie SJ, et al., reviewed the use of probiotics to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in very preterm or very low birth weight infants. The findings showed a reduction of 219 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 274 fewer to 32 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;(10):CD005496.pub5. 7. Topical Oil vs. No Topical Oil Cleminson J, McGuire W., evaluated the use of topical emollients for preventing infection in preterm infants. The findings indicated a reduction of 29 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 196 fewer to 267 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;(5):CD001150.pub4. 8. Topical Ointment or Cream vs. No Topical Ointment or Cream Cleminson J, McGuire W., also reviewed the use of topical ointments or creams for infection prevention in preterm infants. The findings showed no significant difference, with 0 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 58 fewer to 67 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;(5):CD001150.pub4. 9. Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) vs. Supplemental Oxygen Ho JJ, Subramaniam P, Davis PG., reviewed the use of CPAP for respiratory distress in preterm infants. The findings indicated a reduction of 187 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 259 fewer to 93 fewer cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;(10):CD002271.pub3. 10. Early vs. Delayed CPAP Ho JJ, Subramaniam P, Sivakaanthan A, Davis PG., compared early versus delayed initiation of CPAP for respiratory distress in preterm infants. The findings showed an increase of 25 more cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 53 fewer to 1000 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;(10):CD002975.pub2. 11. Immediate CPAP vs. Supplemental Oxygen Subramaniam P, Ho JJ, Davis PG., reviewed the prophylactic or very early initiation of CPAP in preterm infants. The findings indicated a reduction of 30 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 61 fewer to 17 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;(10):CD001243.pub4. 12. Bubble CPAP vs. Other Pressure Sources Prakash R, De Paoli AG, Davis PG, et al., compared bubble CPAP devices to other pressure sources for nasal CPAP in preterm infants. The findings showed an increase of 62 more cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 18 more to 135 more cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022 (in press). 13. Methylxanthines vs. Placebo or No Methylxanthine Treatment Marques K, Roehr CC, Bruschettini M, et al., reviewed the use of methylxanthines for the prevention and treatment of apnea in preterm infants. The findings indicated a reduction of 79 fewer cases per 1000 infants (ranging from 105 fewer to 4 fewer cases). The source is Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022 (in press).
